# Preface {.unnumbered}

A clinical team receives a fracture alert. A research group measures hundreds of spectra from a handful of animals.
An emergency department plans its next shift. This book follows the decision that each of these situations is meant
to support. Readers should find three things in every chapter: a calculation they can retrace, a way to try to
refute their own claim, and a reasoned answer to the question of who may do what with the result.

## Who this book is for

The book is written for medical students, doctoral researchers, clinical research teams and people who review
models. Newcomers start from the clinical question and learn the R they need along the way (@sec-b04). Part I assumes
basic medical knowledge but no programming experience. Readers who want to check a specific result can enter by data
type, method or failure pattern; the navigator in @sec-b28 leads from the starting question to the right chapter.

## How the book is organised

The 28 chapters are grouped into seven parts. The chapter number doubles as a fixed identifier used by the course and
by teaching teams: chapter 9 is B09. Every chapter follows the same pattern:

1. **Case and decision.** One person or role, one question and an action with consequences.
2. **Core reading.** A labelled figure or table, the key assumption and a question for discussion. The core reading
   is clearly marked, runs to about 800–1,200 words (8–12 minutes) and is the required reading in the course.
3. **Lab or decision exercise.** In computational chapters, the complete route in R from inputs to result; in legal
   and communication chapters, reading of primary sources, a role assignment and a reasoned decision.
4. **Counter-check.** A parameter, an assumption or the target population is changed. Predict the direction first,
   then compare with the result.
5. **Consequences for patients and operations.** Ethics, regulation, data protection and security, ordered by their
   relevance to the case.
6. **Look up and transfer.** A reviewer question, a self-test with explanation, annotated primary sources, the link
   to the course and further reading in this book and its companion volumes.

## Data status

All computational examples use synthetic data generated in the chapter with a fixed seed, or explicitly identified
published figures. Every number in the text belongs to one of four categories:

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *synthetic* | generated in the book; describes no real population |
| *published* | taken from the cited primary source |
| *assumption* | value set for teaching purposes that would need local verification in practice |
| *open* | a question the chapter raises but does not answer |

No number in this book describes a commercial product, a real hospital or unpublished project results.

## Reading paths in the course

The course [Clinical Data Science in R](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/) uses selected
chapters of this book as required reading. Readers working through the book on their own do not need the course.

| Course stage | Required reading per workshop | Supplementary |
|---|---|---|
| I · Entry | W1: @sec-b01, @sec-b03 · W2: @sec-b07, @sec-b08 | @sec-b23, @sec-b25 |
| II · Application | W3: @sec-b06, @sec-b09 · W4: @sec-b10, @sec-b19 | @sec-b11, @sec-b12 |
| III · Advanced | W5: @sec-b02, @sec-b13 · W6: @sec-b17 and @sec-b15 or @sec-b18 | @sec-b14, @sec-b16, @sec-b27 |
| IV · Translation | W7: @sec-b22, @sec-b23 · W8: @sec-b27, @sec-b28 | @sec-b20, @sec-b21, @sec-b24, @sec-b25 |

For a quick look-up, the first question decides the route. “How reliable is the alert for this patient?” leads from
@sec-b09 via @sec-b06 to @sec-b21. “May our test set contain images from the same animal?” leads from @sec-b10 via
@sec-b19 to @sec-b27. “The support log contains case text” leads through @sec-b23 to @sec-b25 and on to the restart
decision in @sec-b20.

## Companion books and courses

General statistics is repeated here only as far as a case requires. For the methods themselves, the chapters link to
the relevant sections of:

- [Methods in R](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/) – a method reference for researchers and reviewers, with
  diagnostics, red flags and reporting templates (including TRIPOD-AI and ARRIVE);
- [Scientometrics in R](https://r-heller.github.io/scientometrics-in-r/) – case studies, labs and reference material
  on research literature, reproducible pipelines and responsible metrics;
- [Strategy in R](https://r-heller.github.io/strategy-in-r/) – simulation with explicit assumptions and decisions
  under uncertainty;
- [CTTIR Courses](https://cttir.github.io/courses/) – a four-part biostatistics curriculum in R whose progression the
  course for this book follows;
- [CTTIR Tutorials](https://cttir.github.io/tutorials/) – stand-alone tutorials on foundations, regression, time
  series, Bayesian statistics, machine learning and clinical biostatistics.

Each chapter ends with a “Further reading” section that points to the matching sections.

## Programming

The complete teaching path is written in R [@rcore2026]. Base R is sufficient for the elementary examples; mixed
models, differential equations and process simulation use well-established packages such as **lme4**, **deSolve**
and **simmer**. Python or Julia appear only where a data pipeline, research weights, solvers or interfaces offer a
concrete advantage; a box then describes the original implementation and what must be identical for a fair
comparison. Software and legal status of this edition are recorded in @sec-edition-notes.

## History of this book

Work on the cases, worked examples and chapter structure began in February 2025 and was extended and revised
regularly until July 2026. This edition reflects the legal, literature and software status of November 2026.
